toc.title: Coping is not the same as grounding in safety
Should you feel your feelings during a panic attack?

blocks.p: Can panic attacks get better? Generally, I think they can. They can be overwhelming, even debilitating, but I think there's a lot of hope. Here I want to go over some concepts and techniques to help you cope with a panic attack, and to anchor yourself in your safety state before, during, or after one. I want to help you grow from these challenging experiences so they're not as challenging next time.
We'll cover how panic attacks connect to Polyvagal Theory, what coping is versus grounding in safety, and what the heck to do about all of it.

Panic fits right into Polyvagal Theory. Polyvagal Theory is the science of connection, and also of how we respond to danger. Just for now, way not detailed, our bodies can be in either a safety state or a defensive state.
Let's take it one step further and look at the defensive states. There are two primary defensive states and one mixed state:

ul: The sympathetic state, flight and fight. Think of it as mobility, movement.
The dorsal vagal shutdown state. Think of it as immobility, non-movement.
The freeze mixed state. It's possible to have both primary defensive states active at the same time. When they are, that equals freeze.

blocks.p: So freeze is when your body is prepared to mobilize, in flight or fight, and at the same time it's immobilized. Mobile while also immobile. Prepared for mobilization while immobilized, through perception or through force. With panic attacks, that will probably include being prepared to escape, to run. If you're in your activated flight state but also immobilized, that results in panic. That's a panic attack.

Polyvagal states aren't just thoughts or feelings. There are autonomic, biological reactions in whatever state you're in. If you think about what a panic attack is like, you'll notice all kinds of autonomic shifts, and they're directly connected to the autonomic experience of your polyvagal state. Here are five:

ol: Heart palpitations: a rapid fluttering or pounding heart.
Sweating. You know what sweating is, I'm assuming.
Shaking or trembling, often in the hands and legs, when you get that adrenaline spike.
Shortness of breath or feeling smothered: a sensation of being unable to breathe, or pressure on your chest, like you're being smothered.

Chest pain: discomfort or pain in the chest, more of that pressure feeling. This is often assumed to be a heart-related issue. And hey, maybe that is what it is. That's up to you and your doctor. But with panic attacks, it may not be a heart attack. It might be panic.

blocks.h: Coping is not the same as grounding in safety

blocks.p: The biggest difference is this: when you're grounding in safety, you're actually accessing your body's potential for safety. When you're coping with a panic attack, you're not necessarily accessing your polyvagal safety state. They're very different, and understanding the difference will help you plan what to do next time and set yourself up for more success.

Coping is tolerating. You're trying to get through the panic attack by reducing its intensity until it stops. You're not truly grounded in your safety state. Coping could be distracting yourself with the TV or your phone, snacking on something, reading a book, or getting reassurance from someone nearby. Some of these won't do much in a really intense panic attack. Reading a book probably isn't going to help then. So you might do different things depending on how intense it is.

Coping is dealing with it, managing it, just getting through it. The goal is to reduce the negative impact and the pain of what you're going through. Distraction might be the ideal way to cope if you just want to get through it. There's no mindfulness here. You're not welcoming the discomfort, you're not closing your eyes and mindfully experiencing it. You're distracting yourself.

That is completely okay, by the way. There's a real role for coping, and it might be needed. Get through the panic attack by coping. Then learn from it, and set yourself up for something different next time, hopefully something that involves actual safety grounding.

With safety grounding, you're actually accessing your body's state of safety. It's more than coping, and I'd say it's more difficult. It involves some mindfulness, and attuning to what helps you feel safe and what anchors you in your safety state. Examples:

ul: Going for a mindful walk and noticing your surroundings.
Feeling your muscles move as you release your panic energy through movement.
Using your senses to connect to the present moment.

blocks.p: Safety grounding isn't easy, but practicing it helps a lot. If this is a new idea for you, you probably won't be able to use it the next time you have a panic attack, and that's okay. There are a few things to do before you can realistically anchor yourself in safety during a panic attack:

ol: Experience your safety state. Maybe for the first time. If you have no familiarity with it, getting acquainted with it is your first step.
Figure out what brings you to your safety state.
Keep practicing being in your safety state, regularly, like daily.

blocks.p: As you practice, you build the potential to do it again and again, even during an escalating panic attack, when it's not too much yet. Even during rising anxiety, stress, or overwhelm, before it's a full-on panic attack, you can anchor yourself in your safety state. As your safety state gets stronger, the defensive activation of anxiety, overwhelm, stress, and even panic becomes more tolerable. You're never going to enjoy it, but it becomes more tolerable. And as it does, you'll have more capacity to feel panic attacks coming on before they're full-blown.

It's frustrating, but traumatized individuals will have a harder time accessing and anchoring in their safety state. Their ability to access it is just lower. Otherwise, if they could access it, they wouldn't be traumatized anymore. Trauma really is the inability to access your safety state and stay anchored there. The current inability. I fully believe these things can change.

A panic attack can come on rapidly and seem to come out of nowhere. A lot of my therapy clients say it was truly random. But when we really look at the situation, we can typically identify the trigger, if there was one. And we often find that the trigger was something small, something benign, with a whole bunch of stuff leading up to it the day before, and the day before that. A bunch of small events, each one stressful, compile in your body, get more and more overwhelming, and then the panic attack triggers from that one more thing, whatever it is.

So I invite you to recognize the potential for a panic attack as early as you can. If you can, you can reduce its intensity right away. Even with slight dysregulation, do something, not to cope with it, but to anchor yourself in safety and actually eliminate it altogether before it becomes overwhelming. If you notice a panicky freeze energy building up, you can do something active, like walking around the block. That might be enough to get some relief from the early onset and actually ground yourself in your safety state.

We want to do this early, during the buildup. That's when the emotions are probably more manageable, and more importantly, when you have more access to your safety state. Once it's a full-on panic attack, you have very little access to your safety state, and it's probably more of a time for coping and managing. During the buildup, there's more of your safety state available, more to work with.
So check in with yourself regularly. How's my anxiety right now? My stress? My overwhelm? And I'd encourage you to prioritize practicing feeling your safety state, experiencing it mindfully.

If you can anchor yourself in safety when you have some anxiety, a little panic, or some overwhelm, then when you have a full-on panic attack, it might be less intense or shorter than the last time. Eventually you may be able to welcome and invite the anxious, stressed, or overwhelmed feeling before it becomes a panic attack. You might be able to invite that panic flavor, actually feel it, and do some active self-regulation.
But practice being in safety when you don't have those feelings. Practice being in safety before there's a problem. That's way more important.
If you have to use coping skills, that's totally fine. Just get through it. But then you can shift from coping to actively grounding yourself in your safety state.

Right now, once the panic subsides, you might go to sleep and wake up the next morning hoping for the best. Or the panic energy lowers and you just keep using your phone. Next time, once that initial panic dysregulation lowers, try shifting your focus toward actively grounding yourself in your safety state. Coping is the first step, but the goal is to go beyond it and be more proactive about recovering from the panic attack you just coped with.

So once the intensity goes down, don't just leave it. Don't cross your fingers and hope for the best next time. Do some recovery, and that means accessing your safety state. Do something to lower the activation further, because it's probably still there a little.

For example, if you usually use your phone to numb the panic, stop once the panic activation has lowered enough. And don't ignore what you went through. Give yourself a pat on the back: you made it through. Good job. You successfully managed a panic attack. Then do something to help yourself recover.
This is where safety anchors come in, to reduce whatever lingering panic energy is left. You can also use them during the buildup to a panic attack. They fall into two categories.
Passive safety cues are things in your environment that you set up ahead of time. They need to be ready to roll before the panic attack:

ul: The lighting that feels best for you.
The right sound, or lack of sound, or the right music.
A scent you know helps lower your panic.

blocks.p: You can use these during a panic attack to help reduce its intensity, just by taking them in passively. Have them ready ahead of time, and know which passive cues bring you to safety well before a panic attack.

You're probably not in a panic attack right now. I really hope you're not. So now, as long as you're not driving, ask yourself: What helps me feel safe? What helps me slow down? What helps me breathe a bit easier? If you don't know, use your senses. What do you like to look at? To taste? To smell? Is there a texture you like to feel, or something you like to hear? Maybe my angelic voice is a safety anchor for you, but maybe it's not, and you have to go find something else. Don't wait for a full-blown panic attack to figure out what works for you. Figure it out as soon as possible, and have it ready.

The same idea of knowing what works ahead of time applies to active safety anchors. But these aren't things you set up and walk away from. They're things you actively do to ground yourself further in safety.

Sunshine might be a passive safety cue for you. You don't have to do anything, just be in it. Walking might be an active safety anchor. Exposing yourself to sunshine is phenomenal. Walking in sunshine might be even better. You can mindfully experience what it's like to walk, and what it's like to walk in the sun.

There are a lot more: singing might be your thing. I can't stand it. I like listening to singing, but I don't like to sing, at least not with people around. Yoga, art and creativity, journaling. There are tons of ways to actively ground yourself in your safety state, but again, you kind of have to know what they are ahead of time. The buildup to a panic attack, or the recovery after one, is a really good time to use them.

blocks.h: Should you feel your feelings during a panic attack?

blocks.p: That's a tough question. My answer: if you can handle it, sure. If you can't, probably not.

Allow that defensive state activation, including a panic attack, when you can tolerate it. There is a point where it's too much: you're in a full-blown panic attack, and it's beyond your ability to feel your feelings. At some point you just have to get through it, and you have to cope. But if you can allow some panic, maybe as anxiety or overwhelm or stress, and feel it without becoming more dysregulated, then go right ahead.

For me, the dividing line is curiosity. If you're curious what mild panic or anxiety feels like for you, you might be able to let mild panic activation be present. Curiosity is a really good sign that you can feel your feelings. Other signs are interest, self-compassion, and patience. If you have access to those, you can probably allow some defensive activation and use your self-compassion, mindfulness, and patience to really feel what's happening inside you.

On the other hand, you probably shouldn't allow panic to be present if you're going to spiral deeper into dysregulation as a result. Signs you can't handle feeling your feelings yet include unwelcome or intrusive cognitions, like flashbacks, thoughts of self-harm, or thoughts of self-judgment.

If you can't yet feel your feelings and allow mild panic activation, that's completely okay. It doesn't mean it will be that way forever. Even with panic activation, you can develop that skill, that tolerance. Maybe it's just not time right now.

I fully believe panic attacks can get better, but you have to strengthen your safety state to improve them. As your safety state gets stronger, defensive activation decreases. Your window of tolerance, your distress tolerance, widens. That means you can allow more defensive activation without dysregulation.

To get there, mindfully experience small amounts of anxiousness. When you have lower-grade panic activation, like mild to moderate anxiety or stress during the buildup to a panic attack, that's the time to notice it, and to mindfully experience it while anchored in your safety state. That will further strengthen your distress tolerance.
No, this isn't an easy process, and it isn't a short one. It takes work and dedicated practice. But two elements are key to success in emotional regulation, including with panic attacks:

ol: Practice being in your safety state and build your distress tolerance.
Mindfully allow tolerable dysregulation while anchored in your safety state.

blocks.p: Practice those two things, and that will lead to more success in emotional regulation, a wider window of tolerance, a stronger vagal brake. Of the two, learning to anchor yourself in safety comes first. It's the key to reducing the intensity and frequency of your panic attacks, and of emotional dysregulation overall, the pains of your stuck, traumatized state. It's also the foundation for further trauma recovery work. If you eventually want to directly feel your stuck defensive states, including anxiety, panic, anger, and fear, and get unstuck, you have to be in your safety state to allow those other things to happen.
